analysis.one_liner: Ends a long list of corporate subsidies and tax loopholes, from the foreign tax credit to farm payment caps and cheap public-land grazing.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal more than a dozen corporate subsidies and tax breaks, introduced by Rep. Bernie Sanders with 8 Democratic cosponsors, was sent to nine House committees and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut down a long list of subsidies and special tax breaks: it would end the foreign tax credit and other tax advantages for multinational corporations, cap farm program payments at $50,000 per operation instead of $250,000, end tobacco price supports, and charge ranchers fair-market prices to graze livestock on federal land. It would also cut off federal funding for Sematech, defense technology programs, and the space station, require national park concessionaires to win contracts through open bidding, and shrink the Export-Import Bank while abolishing the Overseas Private Investment Corporation. The bill was referred to nine committees, then scattered among seven subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would keep the money now spent on corporate subsidies and lost to special tax breaks. Small and mid-sized family farms would compete on fairer terms against large operations that now collect up to $250,000 per year in commodity payments. Park visitors would deal with concessionaires chosen by open competition and paying real franchise fees. American companies without special tax planning would face a more level field against multinationals that shift profits overseas.

how_it_helps.text: It terminates the foreign tax credit and repeals the deferral of income of controlled foreign corporations, two rules that let US multinationals avoid or delay US tax on foreign profits, and requires Treasury to use a formulaic method to allocate multinational income.

It taxes large foreign shareholders on gains from selling stock in US corporations and requires withholding on those sales, closing a gap under which big foreign investors could sell US stock largely tax-free.

It cuts the farm commodity payment limit from $250,000 to $50,000 per person, ending the largest checks going to the biggest operations, and repeals the Export Enhancement Program and market promotion program.
It eliminates tobacco price support and production adjustment programs, which had kept tobacco prices propped up with federal involvement.
It sets grazing fees on National Forest and Bureau of Land Management lands at fair market value, ending the below-market rates ranchers paid under Executive Order 12548.
It ends federal funding for the space station, Sematech, and defense technology reinvestment programs, and terminates fossil and nuclear energy research funding after fiscal year 1997.

It repeals the Concessions Policy Act of 1965 and requires national park concession contracts to be awarded through competitive bidding, with minimum franchise fees and terms of no more than ten years, instead of renewing incumbents' preferences.

It cuts the Export-Import Bank's loan, guarantee, and insurance authority from $75 billion to $37.5 billion, requires the bank to charge market-based fees, and abolishes the Overseas Private Investment Corporation.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations and their shareholders would pay more tax; large farm operations would lose payments above $50,000; tobacco growers would lose the price support system; livestock operators would pay market-rate grazing fees; defense, aerospace, and semiconductor companies would lose federal grants and the space station program; foreign investors in US stock would face a new minimum tax; park concessionaires would lose their preferential renewals; and American citizens living abroad would lose the exclusion for foreign earned income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals, agribusiness, defense and aerospace firms

drawbacks.text: It terminates the exclusion of foreign earned income for US citizens living abroad, raising taxes on Americans working overseas, not just on corporations.

Ending funding for the space station, Sematech, and defense technology reinvestment programs, and terminating fossil and nuclear research, would eliminate jobs and contracts in aerospace, shipbuilding, and energy communities, costs the bill does not offset.

A 26-percent minimum tax and new withholding on stock sales by large foreign shareholders could discourage foreign investment in US companies; eliminating the portfolio interest exemption would end a tax break widely used by foreign lenders.

A $50,000 payment cap would also bind some large but genuine family farm operations, and ending tobacco price supports would impose abrupt losses on tobacco-growing communities, though transition rules address outstanding loans.

Requiring competitive bidding for park concessions and ending preferential renewal rights would unsettle established concessioners who have invested in park facilities, though the bill keeps compensation for their structures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper the trade is favorable to taxpayers: ending tax loopholes and subsidies raises revenue and removes advantages that tilt competition toward the largest, best-connected firms. The real costs are unevenly distributed: some defense and aerospace workers lose programs their communities depend on, Americans abroad pay more tax, and some sizable family farms get caught by the payment cap. The farm cap and the abrupt end of tobacco supports are the least carefully transitioned pieces. Overall it is a broad, blunt subsidy-repeal bill whose costs fall on identifiable industries while the savings are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to nine House committees and then to seven subcommittees, none of which ever held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders introduced the Corporate Responsibility Act of 1995 on October 25, 1995, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors.

The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Agriculture, National Security, Science, Resources, Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Banking and Financial Services, and International Relations committees.

Over the following three weeks it was sent down to seven subcommittees, including Space and Aeronautics, National Parks, Surface Transportation, and International Economic Policy and Trade, and executive comment was requested from the Agriculture and Interior departments.

No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on November 17, 1995, more than a year before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, large farm operations, defense and aerospace contractors, tobacco growers, federal grazing permit holders, and incumbent park concessionaires kept their subsidies and tax breaks, since the bill never advanced far enough to threaten them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The subsidized industries the bill targeted

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 8 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; original cosponsors named in the bill text include Reps. Owens, Norton, Hinchey, Romero-Barcelo, and Conyers.

against.name: Republican chairs of the nine referring committees
against.role: Committee chairs in the House majority (Ways and Means, Agriculture, National Security, Science, Resources, Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Banking and Financial Services, International Relations)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote in any committee or subcommittee; the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on November 17, 1995.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent and all eight cosponsors were Democrats, while the Republican House majority that controlled the committees took no action on the bill in over a year.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations and foreign investors in US stock
industries.note: The bill ends the foreign tax credit, deferral of controlled foreign corporation income, the foreign sales corporation exclusion, and the portfolio interest exemption, and imposes a minimum tax and withholding on big foreign shareholders' US stock sales. These are rules that let large companies and wealthy foreign investors pay less US tax than domestic earners do.

The payment limit drops from $250,000 to $50,000, ending the biggest commodity checks, and the Export Enhancement Program and market promotion program are repealed. Smaller farms and taxpayers gain from the savings.

Federal funding for Sematech, defense technology reinvestment programs, and the space station would end, cutting off grants these firms receive. Workers in those communities would lose jobs even as taxpayers save.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers and the tobacco industry
industries.note: The tobacco price support and quota system is eliminated, removing federal management of tobacco supply and prices. Public health and taxpayers benefit from ending the program.

Grazing fees on National Forest and BLM lands would rise to fair market value, ending rates set below market by Executive Order 12548. Taxpayers currently absorb the difference for grazing on public land.

Contracts would be awarded by competitive bidding with minimum franchise fees and no preferential renewal rights, replacing a system in which incumbents held their positions. Visitors would get services chosen on merit and price.

industries.industry: Export finance clients of the Ex-Im Bank and OPIC
industries.note: The Ex-Im Bank's authority is cut in half and must charge market-based fees, and OPIC is abolished. Companies using these government-backed export supports would lose them, while taxpayers shed the associated exposure.
